query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Elevated‐temperature degradation of the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA is governed primarily by fast grain boundary diffusion that promotes selective oxidation of key elements (notably Cr and trace Al) at the grain boundaries, leading to the development of a layered, non‐protective oxide scale under oxidizing conditions and internal oxidation under reducing conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: An additively manufactured, fine-grained FCC high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous elemental distribution, high density of intrinsic dislocations, and superior strength and fatigue performance.
generation.intervention: Controlled exposure of the alloy to elevated temperatures (e.g., 600–900 °C) in atmospheres that are either oxidizing (e.g., air or oxygen-rich) or reducing (e.g., hydrogen- or carbon monoxide-containing gas mixtures).
generation.conditions: Prolonged thermal exposure under well-controlled oxidizing versus reducing gas conditions at temperatures where diffusion is active (600–900 °C).
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries and high dislocation density act as fast diffusion pathways that mediate the segregation and outward transport of elements such as Cr and Al, which in turn controls the formation and adhesion of the oxide scale.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the high density of grain boundaries in the AM-fabricated HEA accelerates the diffusion of Cr (and minor Al) to the surface. In an oxidizing atmosphere, this produces a multilayer oxide scale (with an inner Cr-rich and possibly Al-enriched layer and an outer phase including Ni and Co oxidized species) that is poorly adherent and prone to spallation. Under reducing conditions, the suppression of oxide formation externally leads to internal oxidation along grain boundaries, depleting protective elements and causing localized embrittlement.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under oxidizing conditions, microstructural analyses will reveal a distinct, layered oxide scale (with evidence of spallation and non-uniform adhesion) and corresponding reductions in fatigue strength. Under reducing conditions, although a continuous external oxide scale may not form, internal oxidation along grain boundaries will be apparent, with similar detrimental effects on mechanical properties. Damage is expected to correlate with regions of enhanced grain boundary diffusion.
generation.baseline: The as-manufactured HEA exhibits a uniform FCC phase with fine microstructure and high strength and fatigue resistance prior to any elevated-temperature gas exposure.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under temperature regimes (approximately 600–900 °C) where diffusion is activated. It presumes that the alloy’s initial microstructure (e.g., fine grains with high dislocation density from additive manufacturing) is retained and that the gas environment is sufficiently controlled to be distinctly oxidizing versus reducing. Behavior at lower temperatures (with negligible diffusion) or in mixed atmospheres may not conform to this mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative details regarding the relative rates of elemental diffusion, the exact composition and adhesion quality of the oxide scale, and the interplay with minor elements (such as Ti or residual Al) remain to be fully determined. The dynamics under varying gas compositions may also introduce additional complexities that are not yet fully characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple specimens of the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA and subject them to thermal exposure at 750 °C under two controlled atmospheres: one oxidizing (e.g., pure O2 or air) and one reducing (e.g., 5% H2 in inert gas). After set exposure times (e.g., 30, 60, and 120 minutes), use cross-sectional TEM, SEM, and EDS to assess oxide scale morphology, grain boundary elemental segregation, and internal oxidation features. Additionally, perform mechanical testing (tensile and fatigue) on both sets to correlate microstructural degradation with property loss.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness, composition, and adherence (via TEM/SEM/EDS)
Grain boundary elemental maps indicating Cr/Al segregation
Presence and extent of internal oxidation or void formation
Mechanical property changes (fatigue life, tensile strength) before and after exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the specimens exposed to oxidizing and reducing environments do not display significant differences in oxide scale morphology, grain boundary segregation, or internal oxidation—and if the degradation in mechanical properties does not correlate with these microstructural features—then the proposed mechanism based on selective grain boundary diffusion and oxidation would be falsified.

Our study involved subjecting an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy to oxidation at 400 °C under 10 mbar oxygen pressure for both ex situ and in situ observations. Ex situ observations, conducted using TEM after 120 min of oxidation, revealed a layered oxide structure. The 20 nm oxide layer on the equiatomic base alloy exhibited a composition sequence of Ni-rich (bottom layer), Cr-rich, and then Fe, Mn, and Co-rich layers (outer oxide). High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are typically produced using high-temperature metallurgical routes; however, alternative synthesis approaches based on wet-chemical processing remain relatively unexplored. In this study, a compositionally complex two-phase AgCuCoNiFe high-entropy alloy was synthesized using a precipitation–reduction strategy involving co-precipitation of mixed metal carbonates followed by thermal reduction in a reducing atmosphere. The objective of the work was to evaluate the feasibility of this hydrometallurgical route for preparing compositionally complex alloys and to investigate the structural evolution of the material as a function of reduction time. Quantitative MP-AES analysis confirmed efficient co-precipitation of all five elements, enabling the preparation of a precursor with near-equimolar metal composition. Structural characterization using SEM, EDS, and XRD revealed the presence of surface compositional heterogeneity in the as-reduced state, characterized by Ag-enriched domains.
